items.readable_text:
Content:
Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row.

Content:
Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use any row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a Laplace expansion.

Content:
Across the row [MATH: i,] the Laplace expansion of an [MATH: n\!\times\! n] matrix [MATH: A] is given by the formula
[MATH: det(A)|= ∑_(j = 1)^(n)a_{ij}C_{ij}; = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + ⋯ + a_{in}C_{in},]
where [MATH: {\color{blue}C_{ij}}] is the cofactor of the entry [MATH: \color{red}a_{ij}] in [MATH: A.] Remember the cofactor of the entry [MATH: \color{red}a_{ij}] is
[MATH: {\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},]
where [MATH: {\color{black}M_{ij}}] is the minor of the entry.

Content:
For example, consider the following matrix:
[MATH: [− 1|2|1|1; 0|− 1|1|1; 0|2|0|0; 0|1|0|− 3]]

Content:
To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ([MATH: i=3]) as follows:

Content:
[MATH: det[− 1|2|1|1; 0|− 1|1|1; 0|2|0|0; 0|1|0|− 3]|= ∑_(j = 1)^(n)a_{3j}C_{3j}; = 0 ⋅ C_{31} + 2 ⋅ C_{32} + 0 ⋅ C_{33} + 0 ⋅ C_{34}; = 2 ⋅ (− 1)^{3 + 2} ⋅ − 1|1|1; 0|1|1; 0|0|− 3; = − 2 ⋅ − 1|1|1; 0|1|1; 0|0|− 3]

Content:
So, we reduced a [MATH: 4 \times 4] determinant to a [MATH: 3 \times 3] determinant.

items.readable_text:
Example Prompt:
Using a cofactor expansion along the [MATH: 4]th row, write the following determinant as a combination of [MATH: 3 \times 3] determinants:

[MATH: 10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 4]th row, we have

[MATH: |10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1||= (− 6) ⋅ C_{41} + 0 ⋅ C_{42} + 0 ⋅ C_{43} + 1 ⋅ C_{44}; = (− 6) ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 1} ⋅|2|− 2|− 1; − 2|7|9; 1|− 2|3|+ 1 ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 4} ⋅|10|2|− 2; 1|− 2|7; − 2|1|− 2|; = 6 ⋅|2|− 2|− 1; − 2|7|9; 1|− 2|3|+|10|2|− 2; 1|− 2|7; − 2|1|− 2|.]

Therefore,

[MATH: 10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1]

The [MATH: 4]th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 4]th row, we have

[MATH: |1|− 1|0|2; 0|1|− 4|2; 0|− 2|3|1; 0|0|0|− 1||= 0 ⋅ C_{41} + 0 ⋅ C_{42} + 0 ⋅ C_{43} + (− 1) ⋅ C_{44}; = (− 1) ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 4} ⋅|1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3|; = −|1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3|.]

Now, computing the [MATH: 3 \times 3] determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 1]st row, we obtain:

[MATH: |1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3||= 1 ⋅|1|− 4; − 2|3|− (− 1) ⋅|0|− 4; 0|3|+ 0 ⋅|0|1; 0|− 2|; =|1|− 4; − 2|3|+|0|− 4; 0|3|; = (3 − 8) + (0 − 0); = − 5]

Therefore,

[MATH: 1|− 1|0|2; 0|1|− 4|2; 0|− 2|3|1; 0|0|0|− 1]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Sometimes there are lots of calculations involved in finding the determinant of a matrix using a cofactor expansion across the first row.

Content:
Fortunately, however, we don't always have to use the first row! We can use any row we like. A cofactor expansion across any general row is known as a Laplace expansion.

Content:
Across the row [MATH: i,] the Laplace expansion of an [MATH: n\!\times\! n] matrix [MATH: A] is given by the formula
[MATH: det(A)|= ∑_(j = 1)^(n)a_{ij}C_{ij}; = a_{i1}C_{i1} + a_{i2}C_{i2} + ⋯ + a_{in}C_{in},]
where [MATH: {\color{blue}C_{ij}}] is the cofactor of the entry [MATH: \color{red}a_{ij}] in [MATH: A.] Remember the cofactor of the entry [MATH: \color{red}a_{ij}] is
[MATH: {\color{black}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{black}M_{ij}},]
where [MATH: {\color{black}M_{ij}}] is the minor of the entry.

Content:
For example, consider the following matrix:
[MATH: [− 1|2|1|1; 0|− 1|1|1; 0|2|0|0; 0|1|0|− 3]]

Content:
To compute the determinant of the matrix above, it is most convenient to use a Laplace expansion along the row with the most zeros. So, let's use Laplace expansion across the third row ([MATH: i=3]) as follows:

Content:
[MATH: det[− 1|2|1|1; 0|− 1|1|1; 0|2|0|0; 0|1|0|− 3]|= ∑_(j = 1)^(n)a_{3j}C_{3j}; = 0 ⋅ C_{31} + 2 ⋅ C_{32} + 0 ⋅ C_{33} + 0 ⋅ C_{34}; = 2 ⋅ (− 1)^{3 + 2} ⋅ − 1|1|1; 0|1|1; 0|0|− 3; = − 2 ⋅ − 1|1|1; 0|1|1; 0|0|− 3]

Content:
So, we reduced a [MATH: 4 \times 4] determinant to a [MATH: 3 \times 3] determinant.

---

Item 2 — Example: Applying a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

Example Prompt:

[MATH: 10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 4]th row, we have

[MATH: |10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1||= (− 6) ⋅ C_{41} + 0 ⋅ C_{42} + 0 ⋅ C_{43} + 1 ⋅ C_{44}; = (− 6) ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 1} ⋅|2|− 2|− 1; − 2|7|9; 1|− 2|3|+ 1 ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 4} ⋅|10|2|− 2; 1|− 2|7; − 2|1|− 2|; = 6 ⋅|2|− 2|− 1; − 2|7|9; 1|− 2|3|+|10|2|− 2; 1|− 2|7; − 2|1|− 2|.]

Therefore,

[MATH: 10|2|− 2|− 1; 1|− 2|7|9; − 2|1|− 2|3; − 6|0|0|1]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating a Determinant Using a Laplace Expansion Across a Row

Example Prompt:
Calculate
[MATH: 1|− 1|0|2; 0|1|− 4|2; 0|− 2|3|1; 0|0|0|− 1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The [MATH: 4]th row of the matrix contains three zeros, more than any other row. So using a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 4]th row, we have

[MATH: |1|− 1|0|2; 0|1|− 4|2; 0|− 2|3|1; 0|0|0|− 1||= 0 ⋅ C_{41} + 0 ⋅ C_{42} + 0 ⋅ C_{43} + (− 1) ⋅ C_{44}; = (− 1) ⋅ (− 1)^{4 + 4} ⋅|1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3|; = −|1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3|.]

Now, computing the [MATH: 3 \times 3] determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the [MATH: 1]st row, we obtain:

[MATH: |1|− 1|0; 0|1|− 4; 0|− 2|3||= 1 ⋅|1|− 4; − 2|3|− (− 1) ⋅|0|− 4; 0|3|+ 0 ⋅|0|1; 0|− 2|; =|1|− 4; − 2|3|+|0|− 4; 0|3|; = (3 − 8) + (0 − 0); = − 5]

Therefore,

[MATH: 1|− 1|0|2; 0|1|− 4|2; 0|− 2|3|1; 0|0|0|− 1]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Laplace Expansion Across a Column

Content:
We can also use the Laplace expansion across any column to find the determinant. Across the column [MATH: j,] the Laplace expansion is given by the formula
[MATH: det(A)|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)a_{ij}C_{ij}; = a_{1j}C_{1j} + a_{2j}C_{2j} + ⋯ + a_{nj}C_{nj},]
where [MATH: \color{blue}C_{ij}] is the cofactor of the entry [MATH: {\color{red}a_{ij}}.]

Content:
In other words, the Laplace expansion across a row or column is the sum of the entries in the row or column multiplied by their respective cofactors.

Content:
To find the determinant of a matrix, we can choose to use the Laplace expansion across any row or column, so choose the row or column that has the most zeros, to cut down on the calculations!
